title: Broomstick cluster — working the loops into fans
subtitle: Slide groups of loops off the pin and dc them together to form the fan shapes
excerpt: Broomstick cluster is the second pass of broomstick lace. Once a row of oversized loops sits on the pin, groups of four or five are slid off together and worked with dc into a fan. Each cluster fans open into the finished broomstick lace shape. This tutorial covers the cluster pass.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 3 (1888) — broomstick lace cluster pass. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776 — the grouped-loop fan pass.

glossaryTerms.definition: A group of broomstick loops (usually 4 or 5) slid off the pin together, then worked as a single unit by inserting through all loops at once and making dc stitches into them. The dc stitches fan the loops apart to make the characteristic open fan shape of broomstick lace.

heroPrompt: A finished broomstick lace swatch in ivory DK yarn showing four complete fan clusters — the loops worked off and fanned open — close-up overhead showing the open fan texture.

inlineDiagramTopics.description: Five loops slid off the pin as a group, hook inserted through all five from right to left

content.text: is the pass that turns the loops into lace. After the loop-forming pass, all the oversized loops sit on the pin in an even row. The cluster pass slides them off in groups and works several dc into each group, fanning the loops into the distinctive open shapes of broomstick lace.
All loops are on the pin from the loop-forming pass. Hold the pin in the left hand, hook in the right.
Slide the first group of loops (4 or 5, depending on pattern) off the pin together onto the hook shaft.
Insert the hook through all loops in the group (from right to left, catching all 4 or 5 loops at once). Yarn over, draw up a loop, yarn over, pull through 2 — one closing dc through all loops.
Work (4 or 5 minus 1) more dc into the same group of loops, all inserting through all loops. This fans the loops apart.
Slide the next group of loops off the pin. Repeat the cluster process. Continue to end of the loop row.

items.cause: Uneven number of loops per cluster, or loops were not uniform in size during the loop pass
items.fix: Count loops carefully before sliding each group off the pin. If the total loops don't divide evenly by the group size, adjust the last group or work one extra stitch to compensate.

content.text: Hairpin lace is a related two-tool technique — a fork-shaped frame (hairpin) holds the loops while a crochet hook works the central chain. It produces a different kind of loop strip that is then joined into fabric.
